instances.title: Cooperation and Punishment in Public Goods Experiments
instances.description: Group members may pay to reduce the earnings of low contributors after seeing contributions; peer punishment is used even when costly and in stranger matching.
instances.evidence: Cooperators widely punish free riders even when punishment is costly and brings no material benefit; free riders are punished more the more they deviate from cooperators' contribution levels; with punishment opportunities there is less free riding.
instances.pathology: Some punishment of high contributors; efficiency losses from punishment costs in early periods.

instances.title: Altruistic punishment in humans
instances.description: Altruistic punishment: costly sanctioning of free riders with no future interaction, driven by negative emotions toward defectors.
instances.evidence: Cooperation flourishes with punishment and breaks down without it, even with perfect stranger matching.

instances.title: Antisocial Punishment Across Societies
instances.description: Peer punishment option in public-goods games compared across societies; records punishment directed at cooperators ('antisocial punishment').
instances.evidence: Huge cross-societal variation: some pools punished high contributors as much as low contributors, and in some pools antisocial punishment removed the cooperation-enhancing effect of punishment; weak norms of civic cooperation and weak rule of law predict antisocial punishment. Punishment is beneficial only if complemented by strong cooperation norms.
instances.pathology: Antisocial punishment of high contributors undermines the mechanism in some societies.

instances.title: Punishment and counter-punishment in public good games: Can we really govern ourselves?
instances.field_of_use: lab public-goods game with a second retaliation stage
instances.description: Adds a counter-punishment stage in which punished players can retaliate against their punishers.
instances.evidence: With counter-punishment available, cooperators are less willing to punish free riders; cooperation breaks down and groups earn less than in a treatment without punishment. About one quarter of punishments are retaliated; counter-punishment is partly strategic and partly reciprocal.
instances.pathology: Counter-punishment/feuds erode peer sanctioning; a key failure mode of decentralized enforcement.

instances.title: Covenants with and without a Sword: Self-Governance Is Possible
instances.authors: Ostrom, E., Walker, J. & Gardner, R.
instances.description: Compares face-to-face communication (covenants), peer sanctioning (sword), and both in a CPR game; groups can agree on joint strategies and sanction deviators.
instances.evidence: Communication alone raises yields (repeated communication more than one-shot). Sanctioning alone (imposed exogenously, no communication): net yield rose from -38% to 36%, but after sanctioning costs payoffs improved only 11%; far more sanctioning than subgame perfection predicts, some of it error or 'blind' revenge. Communication plus a self-chosen sanctioning mechanism gave efficiency significantly above imposed sanctioning, with near-optimal yields in some groups, but success varied across the six experiments.
instances.pathology: Sanctioning without communication is overused and reduces net efficiency.

instances.title: The effect of rewards and sanctions in provision of public goods
instances.authors: Sefton, M., Shupp, R. & Walker, J.M.
instances.field_of_use: lab VCM with reward, sanction, or both
instances.description: Contrasts peer reward (zero-sum transfer to others) and peer sanction (costly reduction) institutions for public-good contributions.
instances.evidence: Rewards raise contributions only temporarily; sanctions have more lasting effect; combination highest contributions.

instances.title: Positive Interactions Promote Public Cooperation
instances.field_of_use: repeated public-goods game with pairwise reward/punish stage
instances.description: After each round players can reward or punish each other; in long games with stable identities, reward sustains cooperation.
instances.evidence: Reward is as effective as punishment for maintaining contributions and yields higher total earnings; when both are available, reward increases contributions and payoff while punishment has no effect on contributions and lowers payoff.

instances.title: Achieving Compliance when Legal Sanctions are Non-deterrent
instances.field_of_use: lab public-goods game with voted 'mild law'
instances.description: Mild (non-deterrent) legal sanctions either exogenously imposed or chosen by group vote; endogenous choice activates expectations of cooperation.
instances.evidence: Exogenous mild law fails; self-imposed mild law greatly improves compliance via expectations that others comply.

instances.title: Institution Formation in Public Goods Games
instances.authors: Kosfeld, M., Okada, A. & Riedl, A.
instances.field_of_use: lab public-goods game with endogenous sanctioning organization
instances.description: Players decide whether to join an 'organization' whose members must contribute fully and are centrally sanctioned; organization forms only if members unanimously agree.
instances.evidence: Institutions are formed and raise cooperation and group welfare, but success is not guaranteed: players are unwilling to implement equilibrium institutions (covering only a subset of players) in which some players can free ride, so fairness shapes which organizations form.
instances.pathology: Small organizations that exclude free riders are unstable/rejected (fairness concerns).

instances.title: The Competitive Advantage of Sanctioning Institutions
instances.authors: Gürerk, Ö., Irlenbusch, B. & Rockenbach, B.
instances.field_of_use: lab public-goods game with choice between sanctioning and sanction-free institution
instances.description: Participants repeatedly choose whether to play in a community with peer sanctioning/reward or one without; migration between institutions.
instances.evidence: Initially most avoid sanctions, but the sanctioning institution eventually attracts nearly everyone and sustains full cooperation.

instances.title: Institutions and Behavior: Experimental Evidence on the Effects of Democracy
instances.authors: Dal Bó, P., Foster, A. & Putterman, L.
instances.field_of_use: lab repeated PD with voted payoff modification
instances.description: Subjects vote on whether to adopt a fine-like payoff modification that makes cooperation dominant; compared with random computer imposition.
instances.evidence: The same policy raises cooperation more when chosen democratically than when exogenously imposed ('democracy premium').

instances.title: Reward, punishment, and cooperation: A meta-analysis
instances.authors: Balliet, D., Mulder, L.B. & Van Lange, P.A.M.
instances.description: Meta-analysis of incentive-based institutions (rewards and punishments) in social dilemmas.
instances.evidence: 187 effect sizes: rewards (d=0.51) and punishments (d=0.70) have statistically equivalent positive effects on cooperation; incentives are more effective when costly to administer than when free; centralization of incentives did not moderate effects; punishments were more effective in iterated dilemmas with a fixed group than with re-matching or one-shot play.

instances.title: Communication and Cooperation in Social Dilemmas: A Meta-Analytic Review
instances.description: Pre-play communication (cheap talk) among dilemma participants, face-to-face versus written.
instances.evidence: 45 effect sizes: large positive effect of communication on cooperation (d=1.01); face-to-face (d=1.21) stronger than written messages (d=0.46); the effect is stronger in larger than in smaller groups; communication before versus during iterated dilemmas made no significant difference.

instances.title: Communication and punishment in voluntary contribution experiments
instances.authors: Bochet, O., Page, T. & Putterman, L.
instances.field_of_use: lab VCM with chat room, numerical cheap talk, face-to-face, and punishment
instances.description: Compares communication formats with and without peer punishment.
instances.evidence: Communication increases contributions more than punishment, and once punishment costs are counted only communication significantly raises earnings and efficiency. Chat-room communication works nearly as well as face-to-face; adding punishment to verbal communication changes little; numerical-only messages do not significantly raise contributions or efficiency.

instances.title: The provision of a sanctioning system as a public good
instances.venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
instances.field_of_use: lab social dilemma with contributions to a sanctioning fund
instances.description: Participants contribute to a centralized sanctioning system (a second-order public good) that fines the lowest contributors.
instances.evidence: In 48 four-person groups, members who realized the undesirable consequences of free riding and that voluntary cooperation was impossible cooperated to establish a sanctioning system that assures others' cooperation, rather than trying to induce cooperation directly; low-trust participants cooperated more when a sanctioning system was present.
instances.pathology: Second-order free-riding problem on funding the sanction system.

instances.title: Reputation helps solve the 'tragedy of the commons'
instances.authors: Milinski, M., Semmann, D. & Krambeck, H.-J.
instances.field_of_use: lab alternating public-goods and indirect-reciprocity rounds
instances.description: Alternating public-goods game with indirect-reciprocity rounds where reputation from contributions determines later donations.
instances.evidence: When reputation matters for later indirect-reciprocity rounds, public-good contributions stay unexpectedly high; if indirect-reciprocity rounds are not expected, contributions drop quickly to zero.

instances.title: Third-party punishment and social norms
instances.field_of_use: lab dictator and PD games with an unaffected third party
instances.description: Unaffected third parties can pay to punish norm violators (unfair dictators, defectors).
instances.evidence: Almost two-thirds of third parties punish violations of the distribution norm, more heavily the larger the violation; up to about 60% punish violations of the cooperation norm. Second parties punish violations much more strongly than third parties.

instances.title: A Fine is a Price
instances.description: Introduction of a small monetary fine for parents collecting children late.
instances.evidence: Late arrivals increased after the fine and did not return to baseline when it was removed.
instances.pathology: Motivational crowding out: fine reframed as a price for lateness.

instances.title: Detrimental effects of sanctions on human altruism
instances.field_of_use: lab trust game with optional sanction threat
instances.description: Investor can threaten a fine if trustee back-transfer falls below a desired level.
instances.evidence: Sanctions that reveal selfish or greedy intentions destroy altruistic cooperation almost completely, whereas sanctions perceived as fair leave altruism intact.
instances.pathology: Sanction threat perceived as hostile, crowding out reciprocity.

instances.title: Promises and Partnership
instances.field_of_use: lab trust game with pre-play messages
instances.description: Non-binding promises sent before a trust game; guilt aversion makes people live up to others' expectations.
instances.evidence: Promises increase trust and trustworthiness.

instances.title: The Carrot or the Stick: Rewards, Punishments, and Cooperation
instances.authors: Andreoni, J., Harbaugh, W. & Vesterlund, L.
instances.field_of_use: lab proposer-responder game with reward/punish options
instances.description: Responder may reward, punish, or both after proposer's offer.
instances.evidence: Substantial demand for both rewards and punishments. Rewards alone have little influence on cooperation, punishments alone have some; combined, the effect is dramatic, suggesting rewards and punishments are complements. Demand for rewards depends on whether punishment is available.

instances.title: Monetary and Nonmonetary Punishment in the Voluntary Contributions Mechanism
instances.field_of_use: lab VCM with costless disapproval points
instances.description: Nonmonetary punishment: expressions of disapproval ('points') without payoff consequences versus monetary punishment.
instances.evidence: Monetary punishment sharply raises average contributions (replicating Fehr & Gächter). Nonmonetary disapproval points alone also raise average contributions and earnings, though by less than monetary punishment, showing that expressed disapproval (peer pressure) contributes to the effect.

instances.title: Cooperation under the threat of expulsion in a public goods experiment
instances.authors: Cinyabuguma, M., Page, T. & Putterman, L.
instances.field_of_use: lab VCM with majority vote to expel members
instances.description: Group can vote to expel members; expelled players lose access to the group's public good.
instances.evidence: With the option to vote to expel, contributions rose to nearly 100% of endowments with significantly higher efficiency than the no-expulsion baseline; expulsions were strictly of the lowest contributors; contributions fell off sharply in the last period, when the expulsion threat was unavailable.

instances.title: Gossip and Ostracism Promote Cooperation in Groups
instances.authors: Feinberg, M., Willer, R. & Schultz, M.
instances.field_of_use: lab public-goods game with group reassignment
instances.description: Players can send gossip notes about past partners to their future group members; in the gossip-with-ostracism game, members can then anonymously vote before each round to exclude one participant (excluded with two or more votes).
instances.evidence: The gossip-with-ostracism game produced the highest contributions and earnings; recipients used gossip to ostracize selfish players, and ostracized individuals subsequently cooperated at levels comparable to those who were not ostracized.

instances.title: The virtues of gossip: Reputational information sharing as prosocial behavior
instances.venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
instances.field_of_use: observers of economic games warning others
instances.description: Prosocial gossip: observers warn potential victims about untrustworthy players, even at cost.
instances.evidence: Observers of an antisocial act feel negative affect and are compelled to warn a potentially vulnerable person; sharing the information reduces that affect; more prosocial individuals are most motivated to gossip, even at personal cost. Study 4 shows prosocial gossip deters selfishness and promotes cooperation.

instances.title: The Economist as Engineer: Game Theory, Experimentation, and Computation as Tools for Design Economics
instances.field_of_use: US National Resident Matching Program redesign
instances.description: Stable (deferred-acceptance) clearinghouse design that removes incentives to contract early or strategically, sustaining participation in a centralized market.
instances.evidence: Stable clearinghouses persist while unstable ones unravel; redesigned NRMP implemented.
instances.pathology: Unraveling (early exploding offers) where mechanisms are unstable.

instances.title: Optimal Allocation of Public Goods: A Solution to the 'Free Rider' Problem
instances.description: A tax/message mechanism whose Nash equilibria yield Pareto-optimal public good levels despite private preferences.
instances.evidence: Theoretical: under the proposed allocation-taxation scheme the behavioral equilibria are Pareto optimal, so consumers find it in their self-interest to reveal their true preferences for public goods.

instances.title: A Simple Mechanism for the Efficient Provision of Public Goods: Experimental Evidence
instances.description: Budget-balanced Falkinger (1996) mechanism: deviations from the mean contribution are taxed (below mean) or subsidized (above mean); can implement efficient contributions as a Nash equilibrium with little information.
instances.evidence: Introducing the mechanism generates immediate and large efficiency gains, robust across many experimental settings.

instances.title: Provision of Public Goods: Fully Implementing the Core through Private Contributions
instances.description: Provision point with money-back guarantee: contributions refunded if the threshold is not met.
instances.evidence: Theory: the voluntary-contribution game with a provision point and refunds fully implements the core in undominated perfect equilibria.

instances.title: The private provision of public goods via dominant assurance contracts
instances.description: Dominant assurance contract: entrepreneur refunds contributions plus a bonus if threshold not met, making contribution dominant.
instances.evidence: Theoretical: contributing becomes a dominant strategy.

instances.title: The Role of Market Forces in Assuring Contractual Performance
instances.description: Price premium plus sunk, firm-specific investments (e.g., brand advertising) act as a bond forfeited if the firm cheats on quality.
instances.evidence: Theoretical: quality assured when quasi-rents exceed short-run cheating gains.

instances.title: The value of reputation on eBay: A controlled experiment
instances.description: Buyer/seller feedback profiles accumulate reputational capital that buyers reward with price premia.
instances.evidence: Established high-reputation identity earned 8.1% higher willingness-to-pay than new identities for matched lots; one or two negative feedbacks on new sellers did not affect willingness-to-pay.

instances.title: The Role of Institutions in the Revival of Trade: The Law Merchant, Private Judges, and the Champagne Fairs
instances.authors: Milgrom, P.R., North, D.C. & Weingast, B.R.
instances.description: Law merchant: private judges record disputes and past judgments, and traders query them before trading, enabling community enforcement among strangers.
instances.evidence: Model: the private judge system restores reputation-based enforcement with little information, inducing merchants to behave honestly, sanction violators, become informed, provide evidence, and pay judgments even though each is personally costly.

instances.title: Social Norms and Community Enforcement
instances.description: Community enforcement: deviators are punished by future partners via contagion or label (status) information processing.
instances.evidence: Theoretical folk theorem for random matching with contagious punishment or local information.

instances.title: Opting out of the Legal System: Extralegal Contractual Relations in the Diamond Industry
instances.description: Bourse private arbitration: judgments are kept secret if promptly paid; unpaid judgments lead to the member's picture being posted in the club, notice to all bourses in the World Federation (which enforce each other's judgments), and suspension or expulsion.
instances.evidence: Descriptive: about 150 disputes a year enter the DDC system, an estimated 85% settled in mandatory pre-arbitration conciliation; the system rests on reputation bonds, and the article compares its costs with legally enforceable contracts.

instances.title: Strategic Leniency and Cartel Enforcement
instances.field_of_use: US DOJ Corporate Leniency Program (1993 revision)
instances.description: Amnesty to the first cartel member to self-report, creating a race to confess.
instances.evidence: Cartel discoveries spike immediately after the 1993 revision and then fall below pre-program levels, consistent with deterrence.

instances.title: Leniency programs and cartel prosecution
instances.description: Fine reductions for firms that reveal cartel information, including after an investigation has begun.
instances.evidence: Theoretical: leniency makes enforcement more effective but can induce collusion by lowering its expected cost; in the optimal policy the first effect dominates when the authority has limited resources, and leniency should extend to firms that reveal information after an investigation starts.
instances.pathology: Reduced fines may lower ex-ante deterrence if too generous.

instances.title: Fines, Leniency, and Rewards in Antitrust
instances.description: Compares antitrust fines, leniency for reporters, and cash rewards for whistleblowing cartel members.
instances.evidence: Leniency strengthens deterrence; rewards drive prices to competitive level.
instances.pathology: Fines alone raise surviving cartels' prices; leniency stabilizes surviving cartels; fines used as retaliation between members.

instances.title: Strict Liability versus Negligence
instances.description: Compares strict liability (injurer bears all harm) with negligence rule (liable only if care below due standard) for inducing care and activity levels.
instances.evidence: Theoretical: both induce efficient care; only strict liability induces efficient activity levels (unilateral accidents).

instances.title: Crime and Punishment: An Economic Approach
instances.description: Optimal enforcement trades off probability of apprehension and severity of fines to deter offenses at least social cost.
instances.evidence: Theoretical: high fines with low detection probability can be efficient.

instances.title: A flexible assurance bonding system for improved environmental management
instances.description: Flexible environmental assurance bond: in addition to charges for known damages, firms post a bond equal to the current best estimate of the largest potential future environmental damages, held in an interest-bearing escrow and returned (with part of the interest) only if the firm proves the damages did not or will not occur; otherwise used for repair and compensation. Shifts the burden of proof to the resource user.
instances.evidence: Proposal; descriptive/theoretical.
instances.pathology: Capital cost may exclude smaller firms.

instances.title: The Cost of Reducing Municipal Solid Waste
instances.authors: Palmer, K., Sigman, H. & Walls, M.
instances.venue: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management
instances.field_of_use: US municipal solid waste and container recycling
instances.description: Deposit-refund: a deposit paid on purchase refunded upon return of the product for recycling, combining a tax on disposal with a subsidy for recovery.
instances.evidence: Simulation (1990 data, five materials): a $45/ton deposit/refund reduces modeled wastes by 10%, versus an $85/ton advance disposal fee or a $98/ton recycling subsidy for a comparable reduction; deposit/refund is the least costly policy, and about a 7.5% reduction might have been optimal in 1990.

instances.title: Who Blows the Whistle on Corporate Fraud?
instances.authors: Dyck, A., Morse, A. & Zingales, L.
instances.description: Whistleblowing by employees and other non-traditional actors; monetary rewards (qui tam) strengthen incentives to report.
instances.evidence: Fraud detection relies on non-traditional actors (employees, media, industry regulators) more than investors, SEC, and auditors; monetary incentives explain employee whistleblowing: employees detect 46.7% of frauds in healthcare, where qui tam suits are available, versus 16.3% elsewhere.
instances.pathology: Whistleblowers suffer significant career costs.

instances.title: On compliance
instances.description: Compliance framed as management rather than enforcement: deviations from treaty obligations often stem not from deliberate calculation but from ambiguity of treaty language, limited state capacity, and time lags, and regimes should aim at an 'acceptable' overall level of compliance rather than strict compliance.
instances.evidence: Argument: the level of compliance with international agreements is inherently unverifiable; a propensity to comply is a plausible background assumption; many departures are properly accepted as justified.

instances.title: Is the good news about compliance good news about cooperation?
instances.authors: Downs, G.W., Rocke, D.M. & Barsoom, P.N.
instances.description: Enforcement school: high compliance reflects shallow agreements; deeper cooperation requires credible punishment.
instances.evidence: Argument: high compliance is often because treaties require little beyond what states would do anyway (endogeneity/selection); where noncompliance occurs and selection is attenuated, both self-interest and enforcement play significant roles.
instances.pathology: Shallow treaties: compliance without real cooperation.

instances.title: Achieving Cooperation under Anarchy: Strategies and Institutions
instances.description: Reciprocity strategies (tit-for-tat), lengthening the shadow of the future via issue-linkage and decomposition, and international regimes that aid monitoring.
instances.evidence: Descriptive/comparative case analysis.

instances.title: The Rational Design of International Institutions
instances.authors: Koremenos, B., Lipson, C. & Snidal, D.
instances.description: Institutional design choices (membership, scope, centralization, control, flexibility) chosen to solve enforcement and uncertainty problems.
instances.evidence: Conjectures, tested in special issue.

instances.title: Why Arms Control Is So Rare
instances.description: Monitoring/inspection must render arming transparent enough to assure compliance but not so transparent that it threatens security.
instances.evidence: Evidence the transparency-security trade-off has undermined arms control historically.
instances.pathology: Inspection intrusiveness reveals exploitable military information, blocking agreements.

instances.title: The Hidden Hand of Economic Coercion
instances.description: Threat of economic sanctions to coerce concessions; most successes occur at the threat stage.
instances.evidence: Data show many successful coercion episodes end with sanctions threatened but not imposed.
instances.pathology: Imposed sanctions have low observed success (selection).

instances.title: Sticks and Stones: Naming and Shaming the Human Rights Enforcement Problem
instances.description: Naming and shaming by NGOs, media, and international organizations publicizing violations.
instances.evidence: Shamed governments improve some rights (political) but continue or increase other violations (terror).
instances.pathology: Substitution of violations; shaming can backfire.

instances.title: Promoting Compliance with Human Rights: The Performance of the United Nations' Universal Periodic Review and Treaty Bodies
instances.description: Peer review of states by states (UPR) and expert treaty-body review generate pressure and learning.
instances.evidence: Interviews: UPR perceived as generating stronger pressure (political, peer-based) while treaty bodies stronger on expertise.
instances.pathology: Politicization of peer review.

instances.title: Peer Review as a Tool for Co-operation and Change
instances.description: Systematic examination of a state's performance by other states, relying on peer pressure (recommendations, public scrutiny, rankings).
instances.evidence: Descriptive model of OECD practice.

instances.title: Self-Enforcing International Environmental Agreements
instances.description: Self-enforcing international environmental agreements modeled two ways: signatories, terms, and nonsignatory actions determined jointly (membership as commitment), and an infinitely repeated renegotiation-proof game.
instances.evidence: Theoretical: both models indicate IEAs can do little to improve on the noncooperative outcome when many countries share the resource; self-enforcing IEAs achieve much only when the gains from cooperation are small.
instances.pathology: Large-gain agreements are not self-enforcing (narrow membership).

instances.title: Climate Clubs: Overcoming Free-riding in International Climate Policy
instances.description: Climate club: participants adopt harmonized carbon prices and impose uniform tariffs on non-participants.
instances.evidence: Theory plus empirical modeling: without sanctions on non-participants no stable coalitions except minimal-abatement ones; small trade penalties on non-participants (a Climate Club) induce a large stable coalition with high abatement.

instances.title: Signaling Foreign Policy Interests: Tying Hands versus Sinking Costs
instances.description: Hand-tying (public commitments generating audience costs) versus sinking costs (costly mobilization) as credible signals.
instances.evidence: Game model: in equilibrium leaders never bluff with either signal type; tying hands does better on average but creates greater ex ante risk of war than sinking costs.

instances.title: Norm enforcement among the Ju/'hoansi Bushmen: A case for strong reciprocity?
instances.description: Analysis of 308 recorded Ju/'hoansi conversations (1974, 1996-97): norm enforcement mostly by verbal criticism (put-downs, mild and harsh complaints) by individuals or coalitions, aimed chiefly at big-shot behavior, neglect of kinship obligations, and troublemaking.
instances.evidence: 56% of conversations contained criticism vs 7% praise; costs to punishers relatively low; 170 of 192 threats to community stability were punished by coalitions; lazy or stingy people were rarely criticized and instead lost social regard and exchange partners.

instances.title: Punishment sustains large-scale cooperation in prestate warfare
instances.description: Community-imposed sanctions, including collective corporal punishment and fines, against Turkana warriors who show cowardice or desert raids.
instances.evidence: Representative sample of 88 recent raids; parties of several hundred unrelated warriors; free-riders punished; authors interpret as third-party sanctions sustaining large-scale cooperation.

instances.title: Costly Punishment Across Human Societies
instances.description: Second- and third-party costly punishment of unfair offers in ultimatum and third-party punishment games.
instances.evidence: Experiments in 15 diverse populations: all show some costly punishment as unequal offers increase; magnitude varies substantially; punishment positively covaries with altruistic behavior across populations.

instances.title: To give and to give not: The behavioral ecology of human food transfers
instances.description: Food transfers explained by kin selection, reciprocal altruism, costly signaling, and tolerated scrounging.
instances.evidence: Review of cross-cultural evidence: kin selection, reciprocal altruism, tolerated scrounging and costly signaling each explain some variance in sharing; resource ecology and coordination in acquisition shape sharing.

instances.title: Egalitarian Behavior and Reverse Dominance Hierarchy
instances.description: Reverse dominance hierarchy: followers collectively control would-be dominant leaders through public opinion, criticism and ridicule, disobedience, desertion, deposition, ostracism, and assassination/execution.
instances.evidence: Cross-cultural survey of 48 societies with usable data (from ~316 surveyed): behaviors terminating relations with or removing an overassertive individual reported in 38 of 48, assassination in 11 of 48.

instances.title: The Economics of Roscas and Intrahousehold Resource Allocation
instances.description: Rotating savings and credit associations in a Nairobi slum: members contribute at each meeting and the pot rotates; participation is a wife's strategy to protect savings from her husband's claims for immediate consumption.
instances.evidence: Survey data from Kenyan roscas: mostly women, especially those in couples with independent income; household-conflict model tested with the data.

instances.title: Rotating Savings and Credit Associations, Credit Markets and Efficiency
instances.authors: Besley, T., Coate, S. & Loury, G.
instances.description: Random and bidding ROSCAs allocate the pot among members saving for an indivisible good.
instances.evidence: Theory: neither ROSCA type is efficient; individuals are better off with a credit market than a bidding ROSCA, but a random ROSCA may give higher ex ante expected utility than a credit market.
instances.pathology: Default incentive after receiving the pot.

instances.title: Peer Monitoring and Credit Markets
instances.description: Joint liability makes co-borrowers liable for each other's loans, inducing peer monitoring.
instances.evidence: Theory: peer monitoring (cosigner pays a penalty if the borrower goes bankrupt) transfers risk from bank to cosigner, yet in a competitive credit market improves borrowers' welfare; credited with Grameen Bank's performance.
instances.pathology: Borrowers bear more risk.

instances.title: Group lending, repayment incentives and social collateral
instances.description: Joint liability group lending: successful members may repay for members whose projects fail; social collateral (social penalties) can be harnessed to deter default.
instances.evidence: Repayment-game theory: positive effect (members repay for others) and negative effect (whole-group default when some would have repaid individually); social collateral mitigates the negative effect.
instances.pathology: Joint liability can cause whole-group default.

instances.title: Social Capital in the Creation of Human Capital
instances.description: Network closure enables effective norms and sanctions, trustworthiness via obligations and expectations.
instances.evidence: Theory plus analysis of high-school dropouts: closure supports obligations/expectations and effective norms; lower dropout with more family social capital and in Catholic schools (intergenerational closure).

instances.title: Ostracism
instances.field_of_use: social exclusion across species and groups
instances.description: Ostracism (ignoring and excluding) as a social control mechanism.
instances.evidence: Review: ostracism causes pain, sadness and anger and threatens fundamental needs; targets fortifying relational needs become more prosocial, those fortifying control/recognition needs become more antisocial; chronic ostracism leads to depression and helplessness.
instances.pathology: Can provoke aggression and withdrawal.

instances.title: Worker policing in the honeybee
instances.description: Worker policing: honeybee workers discriminate against and destroy worker-laid male eggs, leaving queen-laid eggs.
instances.evidence: Experiments show strong discrimination by workers against worker-laid male eggs, supporting the worker-policing hypothesis (queens mate with 10-20 males; ~1 in 1000 males worker-derived).

instances.title: Enforced altruism in insect societies
instances.field_of_use: 10 species of social wasps and honeybee
instances.description: Comparative test in nine Vespidae wasps and the honeybee: whether workers forgo reproduction voluntarily or because nestmates police (kill) worker-laid eggs.
instances.evidence: Social coercion is the key: workers forgo reproduction in response to the threat that their eggs will be policed; altruism is enforced.

instances.title: Conflict resolution in insect societies
instances.authors: Ratnieks, F.L.W., Foster, K.R. & Wenseleers, T.
instances.description: Review of conflict resolution: policing, coercion, and kin structure regulating reproduction and caste.
instances.evidence: Review of five areas of reproductive conflict (sex allocation, queen rearing, male rearing, caste fate, breeding conflicts); kinship, coercion and constraint typically combine to limit conflict and often resolve it completely.

instances.title: Image scoring and cooperation in a cleaner fish mutualism
instances.field_of_use: cleaner wrasse (Labroides dimidiatus) and client fish
instances.description: Clients eavesdrop on cleaners' interactions and preferentially approach cleaners seen cooperating.
instances.evidence: Field/lab experiments: eavesdropping clients spent more time next to 'cooperative' cleaners (image scoring); trained cleaners fed more cooperatively in an image-scoring than a non-image-scoring situation.

instances.title: Punishment and partner switching cause cooperative behaviour in a cleaning mutualism
instances.field_of_use: cleaner wrasse and client reef fish
instances.description: Clients respond to cleaner cheating (biting mucus) by chasing the cleaner (punishment) or switching partners.
instances.evidence: Lab experiment: plates mimicking client chasing (punishment) or fleeing (partner switching) when cleaners ate preferred prawn shifted cleaners toward flake feeding after six learning trials.

instances.title: Punishment in animal societies
instances.description: Retaliatory aggression that reduces the payoffs of cheating, parasitism, or failure to cooperate.
instances.evidence: Review: retaliatory aggression is common; used to establish dominance, discourage parasites and cheats, discipline offspring or sexual partners, and maintain cooperative behavior.

instances.title: Host sanctions and the legume–rhizobium mutualism
instances.description: Host sanctions: soybeans penalize rhizobia that fail to fix N2 inside their nodules; decreased O2 supply to the nodule implicated as a possible mechanism.
instances.evidence: Experiments at three scales (whole plants, half root systems, single nodules): forced non-fixation reduced rhizobial reproductive success by about 50%.

instances.title: Evolution of indirect reciprocity by image scoring
instances.description: Image scoring: individuals help those with good image scores, gained by helping others.
instances.evidence: Simulations and analytic models: indirect reciprocity is evolutionarily stable if the probability of knowing the recipient's image exceeds the cost-to-benefit ratio of helping.

instances.title: Biological markets: supply and demand determine the effect of partner choice in cooperation, mutualism and mating
instances.description: Biological market: partner choice and competition among potential partners set the 'price' of cooperation.
instances.evidence: Formal model plus examples of mating, cooperative and mutualistic markets: when one class outnumbers the other and sampling costs are low, choosiness selects for high-value commodities.

instances.title: Chimpanzees are vengeful but not spiteful
instances.authors: Jensen, K., Call, J. & Tomasello, M.
instances.description: Chimpanzees could pull a rope to collapse a table, removing food from a conspecific; tested when food was stolen vs merely unequally obtained.
instances.evidence: Chimpanzees retaliated against conspecifics who stole their food but did not knock food away when the outcome alone was disadvantageous (vengeful, not spiteful).

instances.title: Reciprocal food sharing in the vampire bat
instances.description: Blood-meal regurgitation among roost-mates in wild vampire bats, depending on relatedness and on opportunity for reciprocation.
instances.evidence: Sharing depends equally and independently on relatedness and an index of opportunity for reciprocation; captive experiments show unrelated bats reciprocally exchange blood.

instances.title: The Evolution of Cooperation
instances.description: Three models: directed reciprocation (partner fidelity feedback, partner choice), shared genes, and byproduct benefits.
instances.evidence: Review.

instances.title: Punishment and cooperation in nature
instances.authors: Raihani, N.J., Thornton, A. & Bshary, R.
instances.description: Review of punishment defined by function: behavior that reduces the punished individual's payoff and causes it to cooperate later.
instances.evidence: Review: punishment most probable when players differ in strength or strategic options; aggression yielding immediate benefits may often suffice to deter cheats, explaining the relative scarcity of punishment in nature.

instances.title: Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action
instances.field_of_use: long-enduring CPR institutions (Swiss alps, Japanese villages, Spanish huertas, Philippine zanjeras)
instances.description: Design principles: clear boundaries, congruent rules, collective-choice arrangements, accountable monitors, graduated sanctions, conflict resolution, recognized rights to organize, nested enterprises.
instances.evidence: Comparative case analysis: long-enduring systems share these principles.

instances.title: A Review of Design Principles for Community-based Natural Resource Management
instances.authors: Cox, M., Arnold, G. & Villamayor Tomás, S.
instances.description: Empirical evaluation of Ostrom's design principles, reformulated (e.g., splitting monitoring into user and resource monitoring).
instances.evidence: Principles well supported empirically.

instances.title: Can Catch Shares Prevent Fisheries Collapse?
instances.authors: Costello, C., Gaines, S.D. & Lynham, J.
instances.description: Catch shares (ITQs): rights-based individual quotas of total allowable catch.
instances.evidence: Catch shares halt, and even reverse, the global trend toward collapse.

instances.title: The lobster fiefs: Economic and ecological effects of territoriality in the Maine lobster industry
instances.description: Informal territoriality ('harbor gangs'): fishermen defend perimeter-defended areas, cutting trap lines of intruders after warnings.
instances.evidence: Defended areas have larger lobsters, higher catch and incomes.
instances.pathology: Violence and exclusion of newcomers.

instances.title: Local-level management and the commons problem: A comparative study of Turkish coastal fisheries
instances.description: Alanya (Turkey) fishing cooperative: fishing spots listed and spaced before the season, fishers draw lots for initial spots, then rotate daily through sites (east Sept-Jan, west after).
instances.evidence: Descriptive: rotation reduces conflict and equalizes access.

instances.title: Emergent Properties of Balinese Water Temple Networks: Coadaptation on a Rugged Fitness Landscape
instances.description: Water-temple networks coordinate irrigation schedules (turn-taking) across subaks, balancing water sharing and pest control.
instances.evidence: Ecological modeling: water temple networks reshape the adaptive landscape; presented as a complex adaptive system evolved to manage the agroecosystem.

instances.title: Local Enforcement and Better Forests
instances.authors: Gibson, C.C., Williams, J.T. & Ostrom, E.
instances.description: Regular local monitoring and sanctioning of forest rules by user groups.
instances.evidence: Test with IFRI data from 178 forest user groups: regular monitoring and sanctioning (rule enforcement) is argued and tested as a necessary condition for good forest conditions, compared against social capital, formal organization and forest dependence.

instances.title: Conditional Cooperation and Costly Monitoring Explain Success in Forest Commons Management
instances.authors: Rustagi, D., Engel, S. & Kosfeld, M.
instances.description: Costly monitoring (forest patrols) by user groups combined with conditional cooperator share.
instances.evidence: Groups with more conditional cooperators invest more in patrols and have more productive forests.

instances.title: The Struggle to Govern the Commons
instances.authors: Dietz, T., Ostrom, E. & Stern, P.C.
instances.description: Adaptive governance: providing information, dealing with conflict, inducing rule compliance, providing infrastructure, encouraging adaptation.
instances.evidence: Review: local institutions sustain resources but fail under rapid change; recommends analytic deliberation (dialogue), complex redundant layered institutions, a mix of institutional types, and designs for experimentation and change.

instances.title: Cash for carbon: A randomized trial of payments for ecosystem services to reduce deforestation
instances.description: Payments for ecosystem services conditional on not clearing trees.
instances.evidence: Tree cover loss reduced; no leakage to neighbors; benefits exceed costs.

instances.title: Lab Experiments for the Study of Social-Ecological Systems
instances.description: Communication and costly peer punishment in a dynamic spatial CPR.
instances.evidence: Communication improves outcomes; punishment without communication does not.

instances.title: Performance Pay and Productivity
instances.description: Switch from hourly wages to piece-rate pay.
instances.evidence: Productivity up ~44% (half incentive, half sorting).

instances.title: Peer Pressure and Partnerships
instances.description: Peer pressure (guilt, shame, mutual monitoring) counteracts free-riding under profit sharing.
instances.evidence: Theoretical.

instances.title: Peers at Work
instances.description: Social pressure from observing high-productivity coworkers.
instances.evidence: High-frequency supermarket data: introducing a highly productive worker raises coworkers' productivity; effort responds to productivity of workers who can see them, not those who cannot, and more to frequent interaction partners.

instances.title: Firm-Wide Incentives and Mutual Monitoring at Continental Airlines
instances.description: Firm-wide monthly on-time bonus; autonomous work groups enable mutual monitoring.
instances.evidence: Scheme raised performance despite free-rider threat.

instances.title: Team Incentives: Evidence from a Firm Level Experiment
instances.authors: Bandiera, O., Barankay, I. & Rasul, I.
instances.venue: Journal of the European Economic Association
instances.description: Rank incentives and team tournaments.
instances.evidence: Stronger incentives lead workers to form teams by ability rather than friendship.
instances.pathology: Rankings reduce productivity in some teams.

instances.title: Rank-Order Tournaments as Optimum Labor Contracts
instances.description: Tournament: prizes by relative rank rather than absolute output.
instances.evidence: Theory: with risk-neutral workers rank-order pay achieves the same efficient allocation as piece rates; risk-averse workers may prefer it; heterogeneous ability causes adverse selection unless handicapping.
instances.pathology: Sabotage and reduced cooperation among competitors.

instances.title: Managing Drug Involved Probationers with Swift and Certain Sanctions: Evaluating Hawaii's HOPE
instances.description: HOPE: swift, certain sanctions (short jail stays) preceded by a clear warning for each probation violation; treatment mandated only for those who keep testing positive.
instances.evidence: RCT vs probation-as-usual: large reductions in positive drug tests and missed appointments; significantly fewer arrests at 3, 6 and 12 months; more but shorter jail terms; about one-third the prison days on revocations or new convictions.
instances.pathology: Multi-site replication found weaker effects.

instances.title: Quantifying SARS-CoV-2 transmission suggests epidemic control with digital contact tracing
instances.description: Digital contact tracing: app records proximity and notifies contacts of confirmed cases to quarantine.
instances.evidence: Modeling: sufficiently fast digital tracing could control the epidemic.
instances.pathology: Privacy concerns; uptake thresholds.

instances.title: COVID-19 vaccination mandates and vaccine uptake
instances.field_of_use: COVID-19 vaccine passports, Canada and Europe
instances.description: Vaccination mandates/passports conditioning access to venues on proof of vaccination.
instances.evidence: Difference-in-differences across Canadian provinces: mandate announcement associated with >60% rise in weekly first doses; time series for France, Italy and Germany corroborate; simulated gains up to 5 pp (Canada) to 12 pp (Italy).
instances.pathology: Equity concerns and potential backlash.

instances.title: Monetary incentives increase COVID-19 vaccinations
instances.description: A modest cash payment (SEK 200, about US$24) for getting a COVID-19 vaccine, compared with behavioral nudges, in a preregistered RCT in Sweden.
instances.evidence: Payment increased vaccination by about 4 percentage points; nudges had small positive effects.

instances.title: Nonmedical Exemptions to School Immunization Requirements: Secular Trends and Association of State Policies With Pertussis Incidence
instances.description: School immunization requirements with religious/personal-belief exemptions.
instances.evidence: States permitting personal-belief exemptions and easy exemption procedures had higher exemption rates and pertussis incidence.
instances.pathology: Exemption loopholes erode herd immunity.

instances.title: Vaccination and the theory of games
instances.description: Game-theoretic analysis showing voluntary vaccination is a public good subject to free-riding.
instances.evidence: Game theory: voluntary vaccination cannot eradicate disease because self-interest outweighs slight vaccine risk once coverage is high; perceived-risk increases cut uptake more for highly transmissible pathogens; coverage is hard to restore after a scare.
instances.pathology: Free riding on herd immunity.

instances.title: Randomized Trial of Four Financial-Incentive Programs for Smoking Cessation
instances.description: RCT among CVS Caremark employees and relatives/friends: individual or group (six-person) rewards (~$800) vs deposit programs ($150 refundable deposit plus $650 rewards) for smoking cessation.
instances.evidence: Acceptance 90.0% reward vs 13.7% deposit; ITT 6-month abstinence higher with rewards (15.7% vs 10.2%); among those who would accept either, deposits gave 13.2 pp higher abstinence (IV).
instances.pathology: Low take-up of deposit contracts.

instances.title: Put Your Money Where Your Butt Is: A Commitment Contract for Smoking Cessation
instances.authors: Giné, X., Karlan, D. & Zinman, J.
instances.description: Voluntary commitment savings account forfeited if urine test fails.
instances.evidence: 11% take-up; those offered CARES were 3 pp more likely to pass the 6-month urine test, and effects persisted in surprise tests at 12 months.

instances.title: An Evolutionary Approach to Norms
instances.description: Metanorms: punish those who fail to punish defectors.
instances.evidence: Simulations: norms collapse without metanorms, established with them.

instances.title: Economic Action and Social Structure: The Problem of Embeddedness
instances.field_of_use: economic action in modern industrial society (critique of markets-and-hierarchies)
instances.description: Embeddedness: economic action, including trust and malfeasance, is shaped by ongoing structures of concrete personal relations rather than by atomized actors or generalized morality alone.
instances.evidence: Theoretical argument illustrated by a critique of Williamson's markets and hierarchies program.

instances.title: Collective Sanctions and Compliance Norms: A Formal Theory of Group-Mediated Social Control
instances.field_of_use: groups subject to external collective sanctions (formal theory)
instances.description: Group-mediated social control: an external agent sanctions the whole group, which can induce intragroup control of members (compliance norms) or intragroup resistance to the sanctions (opposition norms).
instances.evidence: Dynamic rational-choice model: group response depends on sanction strength, monitoring capacity, and the efficacy and cost of intragroup control.
instances.pathology: Opposition norms: the group may act against the external sanctioner.

instances.title: Groups Reward Individual Sacrifice: The Status Solution to the Collective Action Problem
instances.description: Status as a selective incentive: group members give high contributors higher status, influence, cooperation and gifts, because contributing signals motivation to help the group.
instances.evidence: Four studies: high contributors earned status, influence, cooperation and more valuable gifts (Studies 1-3); those who received status later contributed more and viewed the group more positively (Study 4).

instances.title: The Emergence of Exchange Structures: An Experimental Study of Uncertainty, Commitment, and Trust
instances.field_of_use: lab exchange market with varied information asymmetry
instances.description: Under uncertainty (information asymmetry about goods), traders form committed exchange relations and attend to their own and others' reputations.
instances.evidence: Experiment: varying information asymmetry produced significant differences in commitment, concern for own and others' reputation, and trust among trading partners.

instances.title: Sanctioning Costs and Norm Enforcement
instances.field_of_use: lab experiment on peer sanctioning of deviance
instances.description: Peer sanctioning of deviant behavior, with metanorms that encourage (reward) people who sanction.
instances.evidence: Experiments mostly support the hypotheses: higher sanctioning costs reduce sanctioning directly but strengthen metanorms that encourage sanctioning, which in turn increase enforcement.

instances.title: Contract Enforceability and Economic Institutions in Early Trade: The Maghribi Traders' Coalition
instances.description: Merchants' coalition: members share information on agents' conduct by letter and follow a multilateral punishment strategy, never hiring an agent who cheated any member, until he compensates the injured merchant.
instances.evidence: Geniza documents show community ostracism of cheating agents (e.g., an agent ostracized as far as Sicily until he compensated); game model shows multilateral punishment is self-enforcing with a wage premium.

instances.title: The Gift: The Form and Reason for Exchange in Archaic Societies (Essai sur le don)
instances.venue: L'Annee sociologique; English trans. W.D. Halls, Routledge 1990 / Routledge Classics 2002 (book)
instances.field_of_use: gift exchange in Polynesia, Melanesia and Pacific Northwest societies
instances.description: Gift exchange governed by the obligations to give, to receive, and to reciprocate, which bind groups into relationships of exchange and obligation.
instances.evidence: Comparative ethnographic and historical-legal analysis (descriptive).

instances.title: Crime, Shame and Reintegration
instances.field_of_use: criminology: crime and social control across societies
instances.description: Reintegrative shaming: disapproval of the wrongful act within a context of respect for the offender, followed by reintegration, as moralizing social control.
instances.evidence: Theory: societies differ in crime rates because of how they shame; shaming within respect is powerful and efficient social control.
instances.pathology: Stigmatizing shaming can be counterproductive and make crime worse.

instances.title: Responsive Regulation: Transcending the Deregulation Debate
instances.description: Responsive regulation: regulators combine persuasion and sanctions, starting with cooperative persuasion and escalating up an enforcement pyramid toward more punitive sanctions when firms keep offending.
instances.evidence: Draws on empirical regulatory studies worldwide and game theory (tit-for-tat logic); also proposes empowering public-interest groups and enforced self-regulation.

instances.title: The Structure and Content of Agreements between the Agency and States Required in Connection with the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (INFCIRC/153 (Corrected))
instances.description: Comprehensive safeguards: states declare nuclear material and keep national accounting systems; the IAEA verifies via material accountancy, containment and surveillance, and routine and special inspections; if the Board finds the Agency cannot verify non-diversion it may report under Article XII.C of the Statute (to the UN Security Council and General Assembly).
instances.evidence: Primary legal text; stated objective is timely detection of diversion of significant quantities and deterrence by the risk of early detection. (Text read at the FAS mirror https://nuke.fas.org/control/npt/text/inf153.html; iaea.org returned HTTP 402.)

instances.title: Hope or Hype: On the Viability of Escrow Services as Trusted Third Parties in Online Auction Environments
instances.authors: Hu, X., Lin, Z., Whinston, A.B. & Zhang, H.
instances.description: Online escrow: a trusted third party holds the buyer's payment and releases it to the seller only after delivery, protecting transactions from fraud.
instances.evidence: Dynamic game model of traders plus profit-maximization model of the escrow provider; derives escrow demand, optimal fee pricing, and adoption; numerical study of viability.
instances.pathology: Viability depends on fee rates and adoption; traders may forgo escrow.

instances.title: The Constructive, Destructive, and Reconstructive Power of Social Norms
instances.authors: Schultz, P.W., Nolan, J.M., Cialdini, R.B., Goldstein, N.J. & Griskevicius, V.
instances.description: Social-comparison feedback: households told their energy use relative to the neighborhood average (descriptive norm), with or without an injunctive approval/disapproval cue.
instances.evidence: Descriptive feedback cut use among high consumers but raised it among low consumers (boomerang); adding an injunctive message eliminated the boomerang.
instances.pathology: Boomerang effect among below-average users.

instances.title: Social Norms and Energy Conservation
instances.field_of_use: OPOWER Home Energy Reports to US utility customers
instances.description: Home Energy Report letters compare each household's electricity use with its neighbors'.
instances.evidence: Randomized natural field experiments with ~600,000 households: average 2.0% reduction, equivalent to an 11-20% short-run price increase; highest pre-treatment decile cut 6.3%, lowest 0.3%; injunctive-norm categories insignificant for low users.
instances.pathology: Effects concentrated among heavy users.

instances.title: The Role of Information in Governing the Commons: Experimental Results
instances.description: Manipulates how much of the shared resource state and other players' harvesting participants can see (full vs limited vision), with and without communication.
instances.evidence: Availability of information about others' actions affected cooperation; communication was more than twice as effective with full information; limited-vision groups without communication saw sharp earnings declines.

instances.title: Stabilizing the Earth's Climate Is Not a Losing Game: Supporting Evidence from Public Goods Experiments
instances.authors: Milinski, M., Semmann, D., Krambeck, H.-J. & Marotzke, J.
instances.field_of_use: lab climate public-goods game (pool invested in climate protection)
instances.description: Players receive expert information on the state of climate research before contributing to a climate pool; separate treatment makes contributions public (reputation).
instances.evidence: Nonzero baseline altruism, enhanced by expert climate information; public investment raised contributions further because others rewarded contributors.

instances.title: Climate Negotiations under Scientific Uncertainty
instances.field_of_use: lab threshold public-goods game modeling climate negotiations
instances.description: Players are told the location (certain or uncertain) and impact of a dangerous catastrophe threshold before choosing contributions.
instances.evidence: A known threshold turns the dilemma into a coordination game and collective action is nearly assured; uncertainty about impact does not hurt, but uncertainty about threshold location makes cooperation collapse.
instances.pathology: Uncertainty about threshold location undermines cooperation.

instances.title: The New Sovereignty: Compliance with International Regulatory Agreements
instances.field_of_use: international treaty regimes (arms control, human rights, labor, environment, monetary, trade)
instances.description: Managerial model of compliance: instead of coercive sanctions, regimes manage compliance through norms, transparency, reporting, verification, dispute settlement, capacity building, and policy review in a continuing dialogue.
instances.evidence: Comparative treaty analysis; argues treaty and membership sanctions are rarely used or effective.

instances.title: Paths to Compliance: Enforcement, Management, and the European Union
instances.field_of_use: EU compliance system, compared with trade, environment and human-rights regimes
instances.description: Management-enforcement ladder: capacity building, rule interpretation and transparency combined with monitoring and sanctions.
instances.evidence: Case study of the EU plus regime comparison: compliance systems combining both mechanism types are particularly effective; those relying on one strategy suffer in identifiable ways.

instances.title: Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer, Article 10: Financial Mechanism (Multilateral Fund)
instances.authors: Parties to the Montreal Protocol (UNEP Ozone Secretariat)
instances.field_of_use: ozone-depleting substance phase-out in developing (Article 5) countries
instances.description: Financial mechanism (Multilateral Fund) providing financial and technical co-operation, including technology transfer, to Article 5 Parties, meeting agreed incremental costs of compliance on a grant or concessional basis, plus clearing-house technical assistance, information and training.
instances.evidence: Primary treaty text; Fund website reports grants of about US$4.3bn across 144 developing countries.

instances.title: Annex V: Indicative list of measures that might be taken by a Meeting of the Parties in respect of non-compliance with the Protocol
instances.authors: Fourth Meeting of the Parties to the Montreal Protocol
instances.venue: Report of the Fourth Meeting of the Parties (UNEP Ozone Secretariat)
instances.description: Non-compliance response list whose first measure is appropriate assistance (data collection and reporting, technical assistance, technology transfer, financial assistance, information and training), then cautions, then suspension of rights and privileges.
instances.evidence: Primary decision text (descriptive).

instances.title: Do Carrots Work? Examining the Effectiveness of EPA's Compliance Assistance Program
instances.venue: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management
instances.description: Federal and state compliance assistance to regulated facilities as part of EPA's enforcement strategy.
instances.evidence: National data on hazardous waste generators: federal compliance assistance increases compliance; no consistent relationship with traditional enforcement; state assistance lowers inspection likelihood for the smallest generators.

notes: VERIFICATION: every DOI was resolved against Crossref metadata (title, first author, venue, year match); none invented. located_via='opened page' = abstract read via Crossref/OpenAlex record; 'search' = existence confirmed via DOI metadata only, with description/evidence coded from domain knowledge of these canonical papers (verifier should spot-check evidence fields for these). WebSearch budget was exhausted early in this session, so no publisher HTML pages were opened; Crossref/OpenAlex APIs used instead. SEED DOI ERRORS in mechanisms.csv: Masclet et al. 2003 seed DOI 10.1257/000282803321455395 resolves to Dupor 'Jealousy and Equilibrium Overconsumption' (correct: 10.1257/000282803321455359); Andreoni et al. 2003 seed DOI 10.1257/000282803321455278 resolves to Walsh 'Speed Limit Policies' (correct: 10.1257/000282803322157142); Cinyabuguma et al. 2005 seed DOI 10.1016/j.jebo.2005.02.010 returns 404 and the venue is wrong (correct: Journal of Public Economics, 10.1016/j.jpubeco.2004.05.011). UNCERTAIN: Hawken & Kleiman 2009 is an NIJ report; DOI is a PsycEXTRA dataset record. Greif 1993 (Maghribi coalition, AER) not included - no DOI found in Crossref. Ferretti 2020 and Bauch 2004 are models, not field evidence. Several entries are theory (Groves-Ledyard, Kandori, Bagnoli-Lipman, Tabarrok, Shavell, Becker, Kandel-Lazear, Lazear-Rosen). GAPS: no escrow instance; no IAEA safeguards primary source (Coe & Vaynman covers inspections); graduated escalation in IR only via Axelrod & Keohane; no gift-exchange (Mauss) or Braithwaite reintegrative shaming (books, no DOI). Exceeds 50-70 target (105) - can be trimmed. CANDIDATE MECHANISMS MISSING FROM SENSITIZING LIST: counter-punishment/retaliation stage (failure mode); endogenous vs exogenous institution ('democracy premium' - distinct from self-selection); provision point with money-back guarantee / dominant assurance contract; rights-based catch shares (ITQ); territorial use rights / perimeter defense; rotational allocation / lottery turn-taking (Alanya, subak); payments for ecosystem services (conditional cash); worker policing / host sanctions (biological enforcement); partner switching / partner choice (biological markets); strict vs negligence liability; deposit-refund (distinct from reputation bond); assurance/performance bonds for environmental damage; whistleblower bounty (qui tam) distinct from leniency; state peer review (OECD/UPR); naming and shaming (international); sanction threats vs imposition; climate club tariffs; audience costs/hand-tying; managerial compliance (capacity-building + transparency); verification/inspection with transparency-security trade-off; law merchant/private judges information registry; joint liability; ROSCA; team/firm-wide bonus with mutual monitoring; tournaments; piece rates; swift-certain-modest sanctions (HOPE); access mandates/vaccine passports; exemption policy stringency; conditional cash incentives for health behavior; digital contact tracing. RESUME 2026-09-29 (web search): 88 instances checked against their sources and corrected where the source differed; 21 instances added (sociology, Greif, Mauss, Braithwaite, Ayres & Braithwaite, IAEA INFCIRC/153, escrow, M66 feedback, M67 compliance assistance). Pathology 'default incentive after receiving the pot' also not in abstract. | part2: williams2007ostracism: Framing as 'social control mechanism' and 'targets often comply' is not how the review frames it; responses split prosocial vs antisocial. Evidence 'larger lobsters, higher catch and incomes' unverified; a secondary search snippet reports stock densities 22-50% higher in defended areas. | part2: berkes1986local: Could not open source; rotation details confirmed only from secondary sources.
